intro.text: This document lists what the game lets you choose and what it keeps track of, visible or hidden, taken directly from the game’s code. Numbers are the values in the code today. “Hidden” means the game never shows the number: you see words, ranges or the results.

blocks.text: Settings you choose on the start page

items: Difficulty:

Regular guy (The full game. Most careers peak in the 60s and 70s; the NBA is common, stardom is earned.) · Reality hits hard (Like real life: most careers end short of the NBA, and those who make it fight for a spot. Every choice counts.) · Shoot for the stars (Built for greatness: every career reaches stardom, and the very top is within reach.)
Fast break (switch):

quick seasons with one tap; every real decision still stops the game, a press conference is one answer, and every tab folds its extra cards behind one button (round 25). Growth is a little faster to make up for the skipped choices.
Sim mode (switch, round 25):

fast break plus the routine calls made for him (the season plan, the summer, national team call-ups, G League assignments, press conferences); it stops only for turning points, offers, the draft, contracts, brands and storylines.
Simple text (switch):
every explanation on every tab is hidden; status lines and a press answer’s tone stay.
Built in a lab (mode):
design a player and spend credits on ratings instead of training (also a mini-game).
Name and jersey number (0–99), dominant hand (left or right), country, hometown and high school (assigned when not chosen).
Position:
PG (Point guard), SG (Shooting guard), SF (Small forward), PF (Power forward), C (Center). Random never repeats the last pick.
Archetype:
five per position (25 in all), each a starting shape of the eight ratings that adds up to the same total.
Focus stats:
two ratings that grow about 1.8 times faster (the rest at 0.85). Changing them later needs a breakthrough season.
Height:
a full-grown height is drawn for the position (below); a young player sees only a projection that can miss by several inches.

chapters.title: 2. How the game decides: the main logic

blocks.text: A plain-language tour of the rules behind the results. Only the main factors are here; every exact number lives in the game’s balance file. Worked examples are given to 6–7 significant figures.

items: Every team has a strength number:
the quality of its roster plus its coach.
The stronger team wins more often, never always:
win chance = logistic((your strength − their strength + home edge) ÷ 4.5). Home court is worth 1.2 strength.
He changes it:
(his OVR − the OVR of the player he replaces) × (his share of the minutes) × 0.25. An 85 OVR starter replacing a 75, playing 36 of 48 minutes, adds 1.875 strength.
Extras add or take away strength:

chemistry, coach trust, star gravity (OVR 84 and up), the winning-player edge (great defenders, floor generals, 3&D), team style, roster fit (round 24), the duo or Big Three, the fans, the city, storylines and midseason swings.
Playoffs are series:
best of seven, game by game, with the same win chance. A small edge per game becomes a big edge per series.
A title is four series in a row,
so the per-game edge is multiplied four times over.
The playoff grind:
in NBA playoff games his team gives up 1.0 strength (every opponent raises its game). At even strength that turns 50% into 44.46719%.
Playoff-only extras:
some fans (playoff edge) and winning players (the edge counts 1.6 times in the playoffs) help more in May and June.

head: Chance to win each game
Chance to win a series
Chance to win four series (the title)

blocks.text: This is why a title needs a strong team around him, not only a great player: one point of strength moves the title odds far more than one point of OVR does on its own.
Roster fit: how the players around him fit together (round 24)

items: Every teammate gets ratings:
his archetype’s leanings around his OVR (85% of the archetype’s shape, a little noise of his own), shifted so they still add up to his OVR.
The team profile:
the average of each of the eight ratings, the starting five (him included) counting three times the bench (the next four players).
Balanced:
how evenly the profile is spread. A spread (standard deviation) of 3.4 rating points is neutral; 1 point less is fully balanced (+1), 1 point more fully lopsided (−1).
Built for the system:
every team has a system (its coach’s, or the style he sets). The lean of the profile toward the ratings that system wants, ÷ 2.5, from −1 to +1.
Shape = the better of the two,
minus 0.33 (the average of that better score, so an average roster adds nothing), × 0.8 strength.
Depth:
his bench’s average OVR against the league’s usual bench, ÷ 3.5, from −1 to +1, × 0.5 strength.
Then the difficulty’s team-factor dial:
Regular guy ×0.5 (never below 0.5), the other modes ×1.

blocks.text: Measured over 1,100 seasons of simulated careers: the profile’s spread was 2.46 (10th percentile), 3.40 (median) and 4.46 (90th); the lean toward the system −2.86 to 2.22; the bench gap −3.44 to 3.78. The resulting bonus at full dial averages +0.025388, with 10% of seasons below −0.724839 and 10% above +0.759937. Worked example: a balanced five (spread 2.9, balance +0.5) with a bench 2.1 OVR above the usual one (depth +0.6) gets (0.5 − 0.33) × 0.8 + 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.436 strength, or 0.218 in Regular guy.

items: Ratings set what he is good at;
minutes and role set how much he gets to show it.
Each game has form:
a hot or cold night (about ±17%) and a streaky rhythm across the half; morale nudges it.
Value per game
(the number the awards use) = points + 1.05 × rebounds + 1.55 × assists + 2.3 × (steals + blocks) − turnovers, plus a bonus for scoring efficiently.

items: Age sets the base speed:
fastest at 14–18, slowing through the 20s, nothing left at 34. Early and late bloomers shift the curve.
Potential is the ceiling:
the closer a rating is to it, the slower it grows.
Focus ratings grow 1.8 times as fast;
the others 0.85 times.
The hidden growth rate
(about 0.5 to 2.2) multiplies everything; fast learners also break through and surge more.
Each half:
the plan, minutes, how well he played, mood and the half’s outcome (surge, breakthrough, steady, plateau, setback) multiply it.
Regular guy only:
above OVR 85 growth slows by 7% a point (never below 40%), so the very top takes work.
Every prospect gets a board score:
55% current OVR, 35% what scouts think his ceiling is, 10% production, minus 1.2 for each year older than 19, plus a little noise.
The order:
a lottery among non-playoff teams for the top four picks (the worst teams have the best odds), then worst record first. Teams pick the best board score, with a little disagreement.
A chance after every game he plays:
base 0.92% × durability (hidden) × the plan × minutes (tired legs) × age (×0.85 under 24, ×1.2 from 30, ×1.4 from 34) × difficulty, more for very tall bodies.
Wear builds up
from minutes and hard plans and raises the risk; recovery plans and rest bring it down.

blocks.text: Legacy and the Hall of Fame

items: Legacy points add up the career:

MVP 9, Finals MVP 5, All-NBA 5/4/3, DPOY 4, a title 3 (4.5 as a key player), All-Star 2, ROY 2, scoring title 2, other stat titles 1.5, Sixth Man 1, 1 for every 1,500 NBA points, an NCAA title or EuroLeague 2.
Hall of Fame:
100 legacy points (about the top 11–13% of Regular guy careers).

blocks.text: How new things change the balance

items: Everything feeds a few levers:
ratings (through growth), minutes, team strength, morale, fame and the body. A new event, plan, stat or feature matters only through these.
Ratings and growth:
a rating bonus from an event counts once; a change to growth (a plan, a culture, a mentor) compounds every half, so small growth changes move peak OVR the most.
Team strength:
one point is roughly five or six points of win chance per game, which the playoffs multiply (see the title table). Features that add strength move titles much more than awards.
Awards are races:
they rank him against the league, so a feature that helps everyone (or the whole league) changes little; one that helps only him moves his award odds.
Minutes:
more minutes mean more stats, more growth and more injury risk at the same time (the round 24 deep-bench change is an example).
Roster fit (round 24) adds team strength only for his team,
so it moves titles more than awards; it was calibrated to add nothing on average, so it changes who wins rather than how often.
Difficulty:
each mode changes potential, growth speed and injury risk, not the league.
That is why every change is checked with the simulation:
thousands of careers are played and compared with the last approved numbers (peak OVR, NBA, All-Star, MVP, Hall of Fame, titles) before it ships.

blocks.text: The last approved numbers are round 22’s. Round 24 changed deep-bench minutes, long careers and added roster fit; round 25 added the systems in chapter 15 (money sinks, staff, fines, press conferences, contract talks, rivals, the news, the one-per-shelf shop). 1,600 careers were played with the smart player and casual mini-game play, as for round 22. The last column is how many standard errors the change is.

Where the change comes from. Titles have sat near 32–33% since round 24 (its 8,000-career check: 32.75%), so the title rise is round 24’s roster fit and longer careers, not round 25. A paired run on 800 of the same careers with the round 24 shop stock (any mix of shelves) shows the one-per-shelf shop takes −0.2552 peak OVR (±0.1776) and −2.8750 All-Star points (±1.1888): a visit now offers one or two training items where it often offered three or four. The rest of the peak drop (about −0.67) comes from the other round 25 changes and was not split further. Options for the owner: keep these numbers; give growth back by always stocking a training item (or two training shelves); and, separately, round 24’s title option (a playoff grind of 1.3 takes about 1.8 title points off; about 1.6 brings titles back near 29.2%).

blocks.text: Hidden traits rolled at the start

items: Potential and caps:
a hidden ceiling for every rating; the scouting grade is a guess at it that gets more accurate with age.
Growth rate:
hidden, about 0.5x to 2.2x; grind plans, mentors, film sessions and early-morning workouts can raise it.
Growth type:
early 20%, standard 60%, late 20% (early bloomers peak young, late bloomers keep climbing).
Aging profile:
durable 20%, normal 60%, fragile 20%; decline starts at 31 (durable), 29 (normal), 27 (fragile).
Durability:
a hidden injury multiplier (0.7 to 1.3).
Rare mold (anomaly):
about 1 in 20 players starts with a rare gift in one skill (point center, shooting big, rebounding guard...).
Natural frame (build):
how far his body wants to sit above or below his best playing weight.

blocks.text: How rare is a 99 OVR? (measured in round 23)

OVR is shown rounded, so a 99 means a true OVR of 98.5 or more, and because every rating stops at 99, that needs nearly every rating at the top. Measured with the game’s own simulation (smart choices, casual mini-games):

Both sit under the owner’s limits (below 2% for Regular guy, below 0.5% for Reality), so the balance stays as it is. Three changes were tested and dropped: letting Reality potentials go to 103 (no change), a wider spread of Reality potential (0.2%, but fewer players reach the NBA: 53.3% to 48.2%), and a rare generational prospect (no more 99s, while MVPs went from 1.95% to 3.75%).

chapters.title: 4. Body: height, weight, wear, injuries, muscles

items: Best playing weight:
220 lb at 6′7″, 6.5 lb per inch taller (less per inch shorter); teenagers carry a share of it and grow into it by 21.
Heavier than best:
stronger inside (rebounding, interior defense, finishing), slower (athleticism, perimeter defense); well over it wears the body down faster.
Lighter than best:
a little quicker at first, then just easier to push around.
What moves it:
plans (Weight room on, Speed and agility off, Recovery a little on), long injuries, events, shop items, city cultures, and a drift back toward his natural frame every summer.

blocks.text: Body wear (0–100) builds from minutes, hard plans, injuries and extra weight, and makes aging hit harder after 30. Recovery plans, rest and health purchases lower it.

items: A hidden longevity score
grows with every Recovery plan (+1 as the main plan, half as a side plan), health item (+2), rest summer (+1.5) and season with body wear under 20 (+1).
From age
32 it slows aging by 1.5% a point (up to 70%) and makes a sudden decline rarer (up to 60% less).
The age ceiling:
from 37, OVR above the ceiling is trimmed (half of the gap each half): 85 at 40, then 3.5 less each year.
Measured:
a durable body kept this way averages 83.3633 OVR at 40 and 52.23 at 50; 85 at 40 is reachable.
Retirement is forced at
50 (an achievement for getting there).

items: Each part is a timing tap:

the green is 0.31 of the bar, +0.005 per athleticism point above 80, −0.032 per point of the part’s difficulty (never below 0.11). The marker sweeps the bar in 1150 ms, 34 ms faster per point of the dunk’s difficulty (never under 520).
Judges:

raw score = 30 + 1.2 × difficulty + 12 × timing quality + fresh takeoff or prop (up to 1.2) − 2.5 per failed attempt. A judge gives 7 from 35, 8 from 41, 9 from 47, 10 from 53, each with his own taste.

a landed move is gone (takeoffs and props can repeat). 10 moves: Two-hand slam (1), Tomahawk (1), Reverse (2), Windmill (2), Double pump (2), 360 (3), Rock the cradle (3), Between the legs (4), Behind the back (4), Scorpion (5).

items: Two buttons:
A blocks and S steals (or tap the two pads). Notes fall to a line on the beat of a drum machine built in the browser; long notes are held to their end.
Every run is new:

the chart is dealt from 14 four-beat sets ("their plays"), easier ones early and harder ones late, never the same set twice in a row, often mirrored. A run lasts 40 to 52 seconds of play at 100 to 124 beats a minute, and a note is added wherever 2.8 seconds would pass without one (the owner asked for a press at least every 3 seconds).
Timing:

perfect within 50 ms of the beat, good within 120 ms; a press up to 200 ms early counts the note as missed, so mashing does not pay. The clock is the sound coming out of the speakers, so presses line up with what the player hears.
Grade:
accuracy counts a perfect as 1, a good as 0.6 and a held long note as 1; S from 95%, A 85%, B 70%, C 50%.
Pays:
perimeter and interior defense (S 4, A 2.5, B 1.2, C 0.5 points before the season scaling, split evenly), and fame for an S. In a career it opens when perimeter or interior defense reaches 82.
Measured over 2,000 charts:

a run lasts 44.95524 s on average (38.4 to 51.72 s), with 88.2315 notes (54 to 126), 1.962652 notes a second and 7.688 long notes; the longest wait for a note is 2.4 s; all 14 sets appear. A scripted player pressing exactly on the beat scores 100% (all perfect).

the result pops up big (+2, +3, BLOCKED!, STOLEN!, NO GOOD, HERE COMES THE RUN) with the moment under it (takes the lead, all tied up, dagger, at the buzzer). A buzzer-beater turns the backboard and the frame red; makes set off camera flashes in the crowd and light the ribbon board in the scoring team's colour.
Look:

a side view of an arena: a dim crowd, the ribbon board, a hardwood floor with the paint, the three-point line and the baseline, the stanchion, backboard, rim and net. On the cam each player is drawn flat: one colour and one shade for each part, for a casual look (the start page and cards keep the full shading). The choice:

NBA, NBA Cup, Olympic, World Cup and the other big finals open with Play the last minutes, Watch them, or Skip to the result. Each kind of final has its own floor, and the other side wears its own colours (a nation’s for national teams).
Playing:
before each of his team’s baskets (and each of its stops), pick a move: three for a three, four for a two, two for a stop. Then stop the meter.
The meter:

a marker sweeps there and back every 1.3 seconds; the green is 0.14 of the bar plus 0.18 × (the move’s rating ÷ 100), centred somewhere in the middle half; its middle 36% is a perfect. Space, Enter or a tap stops it.
What it changes:

the result is settled by the season (the title, the awards and the bracket depend on it), so each play scores as written; the move and the timing change how it is told and earn a clutch rating (perfect 3, good 2, lucky 1 point a play, as a share of the best possible). Reputation + rating ÷ 25 (rounded down), mood +3 from 70, and achievements.

Plans what you eat, so the weight stays where it should and the body ages slower.
A little more athleticism every season.
Fewer injuries, and less wear on the body.
A little better shooting and a little more range every season.
A little better handle and weak hand every season.
Keeps your head right: a lift in morale every season.
Film on every opponent: a little more feel for the game every season.
Better sleep: the body ages a little slower and gets hurt a little less.

items: Hiring:
a turning point offers each role in a pro league; at most 6 on the staff, and only with a bank that can pay 4 seasons.
Pay and raises:
paid from the bank every season (whoever cannot be paid leaves). A raise moves him up a level: pay ×1 / ×1.7 / ×2.6, help ×1 / ×1.5 / ×2.
Talking:
stopping by once a season gets a line from him and +1 morale.
Art:
each is drawn at work in the role’s uniform: a kitchen, a health club, the clinic, a practice court, a study, a film room, a bedroom.
Measured (400 careers):
1.695 hires a career; 82.75% of careers hire someone.
When:
each pro game he plays: 0.2% a game, ×1.8 with low morale, ×1.4 for a star, at most 2 a season.
What for:
a technical, a flagrant, criticising the referees, a skipped media session, a late bus, a uniform violation, the ball into the stands; NBA amounts from $2K to $100K, 15% of that abroad.
On screen:
like an injury: a page with a letter from the league office and the amount, out of the bank.
Measured (400 careers):
2.2625 fines a career, $51.80K in all on average.
When:
in the summer after a season with a story (a title, a lost final, a big award, a long injury, a slump of 3 OVR, a move, a contract year), no sooner than 2 or 3 seasons after the last.
Questions:
2 after the biggest stories (title, lost-final, award), 1 after the rest. Each answer weighs 3 ÷ questions, so a press conference moves things as much as three answers once did.
Humble:
+2 coach trust, +0.5 reputation and +0.1 team strength next season, per three answers’ worth.
Confident:
+1.5 reputation and +2 morale.
Fiery:
+2.5 reputation, -2 trust, a 20% chance of a fine, and next season’s locker room catches fire or splits (±0.15).
The crowd:
demanding NBA crowds love fire, friendly ones humility, the rest confidence; a match adds +1 reputation and morale.
Fast break and sim:
fast break makes it one answer whose tone carries through; sim answers humbly on its own.
Where:
under every pro offer not on a fixed scale (rookie deals, minimums and camp deals are fixed): More money (+15%), One more year (up to 5) or A bigger role (one step). 2 asks an offer.
The answer:

the team’s hidden patience is 0.35, plus reputation ÷ 220, plus his OVR above the league average ÷ 45, less 0.2 for each ask before. A yes gives the whole ask, a meet-halfway half of it (money only), and an out-of-patience team pulls the offer.
Measured (2,000 tries each, average OVR, first money ask):
accepted 33.95%, 47.15% and 62.05% of the time at reputation 30, 60 and 90; pulled 35.20%, 27.95% and 20.55%.
One at a time, and the rivalry only grows:

in his first NBA season, the best rookie at his position; once he starts, the closest player at his position on a real NBA rival team; once he is top five in an MVP race and someone has beaten him for big awards twice, that player.
What is kept:
the head to head (every game between their teams, playoffs too), both OVRs season by season and a line on what happened. If the rival retires, it ends.
Measured (200 careers):
all 157 that reached the NBA had a rival (43 draft class, 91 head to head, 23 MVP); 13.22 games against him on average, 55.35% won.

blocks.text: At the end of every pro season the papers read it: trade rumours come with low trust, a losing team or a contract year; MVP buzz with a top-five race; questions about the body with long injuries; a breakout with +4 OVR; doubts with −3. Around the league opens with what they wrote about him, a power ranking, and under each league story a line on what it means for him.
The shop, the wardrobe and the collection

items: The shop:

196 items on six shelves (Shoes 9, Gear 25, Training 51, Recovery 28, Lifestyle 43, Accessories 40), up to $400M. Each visit shows one item from each shelf; things costing 1% of the bank or more are favoured, so a rich player sees rich things.
Accessories:

headbands (+1 morale), shooting sleeves (+0.2 shooting), wristbands (+0.2 playmaking) and leg sleeves (0.5% fewer injuries), ten colours each, drawn on the player at once; the wardrobe swaps or removes them, and none is sold twice.
The collection:
everything bought, by shelf, with its icon; 34 lasting things can be visited once a season (+2 morale, +1 reputation for the public ones).
Money events:
family requests, investments and legacy projects come up more often; a legacy project adds 3 legacy points. 22.25% of careers fund one.
Measured over 160 smart careers against the end of round 24:

12.818879 clicks a season then; 13.893398 with this round’s first version (+1.074519, mostly press conferences at +0.8464); 13.368080 now that a press conference asks one question (two after the biggest stories). This round adds 0.549201 clicks a season, inside the owner’s 0.5 to 0.7.
Fast break:
with a test career the five tabs show 15 cards and 1,366 words instead of 41 cards and 6,214 words; the Player tab is 1,216 pixels tall instead of 7,465.
Sound:

made in the browser (no files): clicks, a fanfare for a title, awards, injuries, fines, coins, a nickname, cameras at a press conference, a deal, a pulled offer, a staff chat, a visit, a brand jingle, a perfect release; and a four-bar loop while a career is on screen. Effects on, music off to start.
Contrast:

every piece of text on the five tabs, in both themes, was measured against its background (WCAG 4.5:1, 3:1 for large text): the light theme’s orange is a shade deeper (white on it 5.63:1), and gold and amber tags use dark ink.
Keyboard:
the F, G and M shortcuts are gone (the switches are on How you play and in Settings); every control can be reached with Tab and shows a focus ring.
